utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I apologise that the Chamber is a little late. I was caught up in a conference with other Judges and not able to get free in time to be here when I should have been. May I remind you, Doctor, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The question for the witness: Would you please be so kind and determine for us the exact time when the Europe international observers arrived in front of the hospital on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representative of the International Red Cross whom I saw, Mr. Borsinger, was talking to Major Sljivancanin. I believe this happened between 1.00 and 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next question: Did they arrive together with those two military APCs that you described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure. I don't remember. After the captain came out, Dr. Bosanac, Marin Vidic, and myself were confused because Dr. Bosanac said she had received information from Zagreb that Major Sljivancanin would surrender the hospital or hand the hospital over to the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you for a second, please. You're not really answering my question, are you? The fact that you were confused at the time does not mean you can't answer my question now. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Can you please repeat that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I will. These monitors, did they arrive together with those two APCs?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You might as well have said so right away. Did you personally know Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not personally know Mr. Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But I think that in your testimony, when answering questions by the Prosecutor, you did, in fact, say that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned his name. The reason being that when negotiations were held in Zagreb between the International Red Cross, the European Commission Monitoring Mission, and the representatives of the Croatian government, it was agreed that Mr. Borsinger would be present on behalf of the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean you didn't know him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you don't remember whether he arrived with those two APCs, can you please describe how he arrived, if in fact you saw him arrive at all.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say that but you interrupted me. I spoke to Dr. Bosanac, and we were both surprised that those people were supposed to arrive were not arriving. At that very moment, in front of us at the entrance to the hospital, there were Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Nikola Borsinger, but I don't remember how they arrived, by what means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how Borsinger and his men left?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the conversation that I talked about in chief, we went into the hospital. Mr. Borsinger did not enter the hospital with us, and I have no idea how he went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: As you described yesterday, you went straight down to the basement?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any electricity in the basement?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When did electricity arrive, if at all, in the basement while you were at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were at the hospital until the 20th, then we were taken away and captured. The electricity had not arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then offer a logical explanation, for your own sake in fact and for the sake of the Court. How come that people that you had christened as Chetniks and the nature -- and the captain who was with Kuzmic were able to select prisoners in the darkness of that basement, and you claim there were over 500 people there? How long did it take them to observe their faces and to assess who were the wounded down there in the dark?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were batteries and lamps, electrical torches in the hospital which they used. Candles were lit, too. You could pass through the corridor. You could look at people's faces, and you could tell the wounded from the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that's sufficient. The soldiers you described as arriving with Captain Radic, can you describe what sort of uniform they were wearing? Were those olive-drab or camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the captain and the soldier accompanying him, he was wearing an olive-drab uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I was asking about the soldiers securing the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm about to say that. The captain was wearing a camouflage uniform, but the soldiers who arrived first were also in camouflage uniform. And as I said, they were the first to seize control of the ten entrances to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any additional insignia, such as feathers, something like that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any such details. I don't remember seeing any such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What sort of caps were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look closely enough to see. I didn't look at their caps closely enough to be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Those soldiers, did they go around the hospital searching for something, because you did say that you saw them moving about the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was dark and I couldn't see whether they were searching for something around the hospital, but I did see them take control of the entrances. You could still see that because there was still sufficient daylight for you to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: After the Borsinger's and Sljivancanin's conversation what became of Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question. We went to the basement. I have no idea what he did after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You testified that Captain Radic returned on the 19th of November between 8.00 and 9.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's what you said. You also said that he arrested you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That he gave you some orders that you had to abide by?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to stay close and to remain in that room that I pointed out to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that on the 18th of November, you were in fact not rested at all?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: November.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a physician and you were free. Were you in a position to get in touch with Dr. Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she had left to attend talks with Lieutenant Colonel, if memory serves, Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Vesna Bosanac was attending talks with Mrksic on the 18th, on the afternoon of the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have mixed up the dates, but that's how I remember it to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you -- you had the days mixed up. But my question is: Since Vesna Bosanac was not in the hospital, were you deputising for her?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for anyone to stand in for her. As I said, when the soldiers arrived and took control of the hospital, we had been divested of any power that we had over the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question. What I said was: Before the army arrived, were you her deputy?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So who was?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How come you don't know?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was there throughout and there was no need at any point in time for anyone to deputise. There would have been no need under those conditions; that was the last thing that we were thinking about at the time. I'm not sure if she had one, and if indeed she did, that certainly wasn't me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at what time gaseous gangrene occurred?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think gaseous gangrene occurred in the second half of October when we started running out of medicines, medical supplies, and the corridors were filling up with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who operated on the soldier Boban Gacic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically who operated on whom, individually, in relation to each of the wounded or their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of that soldier, Boban Gacic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure who asked me, but I'm -- I'm familiar with the name. The family name rings a bell. However, I would be going too far if I said for certain. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: May I remind you, then, that there is a statement to the effect that he succumbed to gaseous gangrene after a leg surgery?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That refreshes my memory. Unfortunately happened to be one of those five wounded soldiers in those difficult conditions. It was impossible to obtain medicine for gangrene. You couldn't bring anything into the hospital or take anything out of the hospital on account of the occupation by the JNA and paramilitary units. So we had no medicine to work with. Unfortunately, the result was that people died of gangrene, even those whose lives might otherwise have been saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How, then, did you succeed in sending to the atomic shelter of Borovo Komerc wounded members of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borovo Komerc, the warehouse, is not outside Vukovar. The antigangrene serum is something you couldn't find in Vukovar. It wasn't available and the hospital didn't have it. You had to leave Vukovar in order to get some.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I was referring a while ago when I dropped that name to JNA soldiers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The soldier that I asked you about, was he a JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you say so. You probably have all the information needed to draw that conclusion, but personally I couldn't confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I think the interpreter will be exhausted in a moment if we keep up the present pace. Could you just try to pause in between question and answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already made a pause while listening to your words, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave the hospital at all over those three months?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over those three months, I seldom left the hospital. If I did, I only left to go to the basement where my family were, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did your family stay in that basement?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family was in the basement of the building in which I owned a flat, and they were there together with the other residents facing dreadful conditions. I believe they all arrived in the hospital on the afternoon of the 17th, which, if memory serves me, was a Sunday. I'm referring to the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm speaking Croatian and we use two different words, so please show some respect for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you talking about your wife?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my mother-in-law. As well as the other neighbours, the Uzelacs, the Milosevics, the Koningsknechts. It's the part of the building that we shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Did you ever leave the hospital again for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the MUP building, the police building?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went perhaps once or twice. There were wounded there, but the hospital building is in the vicinity of the police building so there was no distance between the two buildings, and I went there to dress the wounded, to dress their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think that now you have given a very logical answer, so I would like you to describe to the Trial Chamber what you mean when you say that the MUP was adjoining the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital was completely destroyed because of the shelling and the anti -- actually the nuclear shelter, which was the old corridor in the old hospital, was used in order to cover the distance and to find oneself in the MUP premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean, if I understood you correctly, that it was not necessary to cover a cleared area or a clearing of 200 metres in order to reach the shelter?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. You could not use the underground corridors throughout that whole time. You had to come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time that you are describing, was it possible at that time to walk three metres and to enter the MUP, just like you said before?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say three metres. And also, you had to pass through an open area for some of the time between the old hospital building and the MUP. You really had to walk through an open area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I am looking at the transcript, and you said three metres.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least three metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was probably -- the distance was probably even greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe it was four?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not four. Maybe it was ten. I didn't measure it. I'm not a land surveyor, so I'm not really all that specialised in the different distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you a witness on the 18th of November when the JNA soldiers were relieved by, as you said, paramilitary forces? Did you see that for yourself?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it for myself because they came in, so this is what we saw when we were inside. I didn't see that outside because I didn't go out, but from inside you could see through apertures that the camouflaged dressed uniforms were -- camouflage uniformed dress soldiers were leaving and that the reserve forces were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And how many reserve forces did you see come in?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was dark so I really couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How could you see that they were reservists in the dark?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could tell the difference between camouflage uniforms and other uniforms; that much you could see from inside. And secondly, they were coming into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were you precisely when Captain Kuzmic was touring the hospital? Where were you exactly?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Kuzmic and the captain were touring the hospital, I was in front of the office or, better put, that small room when Kuzmic and the captain came in, Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What small room do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I was detained in the day after. I showed that on the diagram that we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the room used by the Crisis Staff of the hospital before that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that the hospital had a Crisis Staff there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was across the road in a different building, in an old building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Well, so that I wouldn't interrupt you all the time, could you please answer a little more briefly and we will easily then come to the truth, your truth which you would like to tell the Court. So where was this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, the Crisis Staff -- well, the hospital had its administrative section and the medical part. The Crisis Staff met in the old part of the building where the administrative offices were, and that is across the street from the old part of the hospital. The two buildings are some four or five metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So how do you know that they met there if you were not a member?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how could I not know? When after the meetings of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Matos who were members of the Crisis Staff would say that there had been a meeting, because according to the decision of the director or administrator, Dr. Matos became a member of the hospital Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what did Dr. Bosanac tell you? Did she go to any other meetings of the Crisis Staff in town?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that. It's possible but as I say, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Now let us go back briefly to the 18th of November, when these reservists came in, according to what you said. If I were to tell you that Dr. Vesna Bosanac, in her testimony before this Tribunal, stated that nothing was happening in the hospital on the 18th of November. If I were to tell you that the head nurse -- I'm not going to give you her first and last name, but she was the head nurse of the surgical ward, said that there were no incidents at all, although the doctor who worked at the ear, throat, and nose ward, who testified here, said that the people behaved properly, that they gave cigarettes. Would you agree with me when I tell you what they said, that this image that they drew for the Court is very different from the one that you are describing to the Court, primarily in describing this behaviour of this Bogdan Kuzmic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Dr. Vesna Bosanac stated as well as Binazija Kolesar, even though you didn't mention her, and as you -- but you did say it was the head nurse of the surgical department. I don't know what it is that they saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So it's not true what they saw?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I saw and what I saw in the places where I was. As I said earlier, if you remember, I think that Dr. Vesna Bosanac on the 18th or after that went to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't want to go through the entire statement now, but she explained her presence on the 18th of November. But since you do not wish to change your position, then later we will assess whether these three witnesses are speaking the truth or whether you are talking -- speaking the truth about the same set of circumstances. You also stated that the objective of the captain and Kuzmic was to pick out the civilians and the wounded who were later to be killed at Ovcara. How could you at that point in time have that impression about their conduct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, in the evening, when I was doing my patient rounds, they said that Mr. Radic, Captain Radic, and Bogdan Kuzmic had been there earlier and they told me what I have already said before - I don't want to repeat that - that they had mistreated them and so on. The wounded were afraid about what was going to happen as a result of this abuse and these threats. They were afraid of what was going to happen the next day or the day after. That was certainly the cause on the basis of which it could be concluded that at the time they were actually picking out people that they were going to propose for the transport, which ended up, unfortunately, in the way that we know it ended. It ended at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So are you concluding now that that evening you didn't know about those reasons on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that they were abused on the 18th and what the atmosphere was like and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We heard that. We heard that.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, I would like to complete my thought. There was panic, there was fear, a very heavy atmosphere. People had lost any hope of surviving, especially some of the people there who were specially abused because Bogdan Kuzmic earlier worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, I cannot allow you to speak for an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, I understand the difficulties of cross-examination but neverthe -- and also the witness answering the question, but the witness must be allowed to answer the question. He's been interrupted now three or four times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, the witness is still answering the question as he understands the matter. It may not be the sort of answer you want, but he should be allowed to give it. Sorry we have interrupted you, Doctor. Had you finished what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for protecting me. I will try to be as concise as I can and to take as little time as possible to explain and also to respond to the Defence counsel's questions. On the 18th, after Captain Radic and Bogdan Kuzmic went to see all the seriously wounded people at the hospital, I also did my rounds with a torch and a candle to avoid confusion that some people had electricity and the others didn't, and there was panic amongst the wounded that they would be killed, specially those who were particularly picked out by those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked a simple question several times now, and now I'm also getting very detailed, long answers. It's very simple. Did he know on the 18th that those people would be taken to Ovcara and executed? That's the question: Did you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you would like me to give you the answers that you would want me to give you, then that will not be the truth. I'm speaking only the truth, and I will continue to do so regardless of whether that suits either side in this proceeding. On the 18th, in the evening, I described the atmosphere for you amongst the wounded in the hospital, and even amongst the staff, because on the 17th, a large number of people from the basement came to the hospital. There was panic and fear because people were worried about all the horrible things that they had heard. They were afraid of what was coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not want to you warn me but this is really excessive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, could you focus on the question which was put to you by Mr. Borovic? It was: Did you know on the 18th that these people would be taken to Ovcara and executed? Now, could you give us your answer to that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That evening, after I did my rounds and after the patients told me what they told me, I couldn't know what would happen on the 20th and who would be taken to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us exactly what time did Bogdan Kuzmic come?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in the afternoon. I really don't remember exactly what time it was, but it was already getting dark, which means that it was probably shortly before nightfall. So on the 18th of November, and that's going to be the same date in a few days, and then you could tell approximately what time it was. At the time I didn't actually have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when Captain Radic came, at what time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic and Kuzmic came together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Together. Thank you. Did the JNA return later? Did they come back again after the reservists had come or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the next day, on the 19th, the JNA returned, as I said before, if I remember correctly, but I really cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And what was the time approximately? Because in your statement, you specified the exact timings regarding the 19th of November. So perhaps you could repeat that for us. When did the JNA reappear again on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the point in time when Captain Radic came and he addressed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will have to interrupt you. I'm not asking you that. Who relieved the reservists? Did the JNA soldiers come back on the 19th and did they relieve the reservists, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I only remember what was happening to me and to the injured in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So can we agree that you did not see that the JNA returned to the hospital again?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you certainly yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that when the reservists were there, some people were taken away, including Marko Mandic.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What day was that and at what time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because I was already detained. I was already under guard in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So if you were already captured, how do you know that they were taken away?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because in the evening, when I did the rounds, I was told that Marko Mandic was not there or the ambulance driver, that they had been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that on the 19th, in the evening, was the first time that you learned that Marko Mandic was not there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th, in the evening, as I said, I learned, and I confirm what you have just now said, that that was the time when I found out that Marko Mandic was not there and the ambulance driver was not there either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name of any other ambulance driver who was missing except that one?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ilija Azasanin [phoen], Mihajlo Zera. There must have been others, but these are the ones that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday about the first time the JNA appeared in the hospital. Was there a major who arrived with the captain? And you said you didn't remember and that no major came with the captain. What can you tell us now?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you this. You told me that there was a captain who came and a major who came, and you told me their last names. And I said No, that wasn't the major who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a different one who came?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Captain Radic came in, he was followed - and this is something that I've already talked about - by Major Veselin Sljivancanin and there was that discussion they had with Mr. Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But that wasn't my question. Before Major Sljivancanin appeared -- and you submit that Captain Radic had appeared before him. So my question is: At the same time as Captain Radic, did Major Sljivancanin also arrive in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen Major in the hospital at the time. We are talking about the 18th. That's what we are talking about. The 18th of November, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I read your book very carefully, the book you published, which you accepted as your own work, recognised as your own work. If I tell you that on page 139 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the evidence of the doctor to be that only part of that book was his own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct. That is precisely the part that I'm showing. He said yesterday: "I abide by my sections." And the other sections of the book are accounts of people who were arrested, and he said that he couldn't stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to make the book more easily, more readily, readable, the editor simply removed some of the comments that were made, even my own. I did make additional remarks to show that the original meaning had been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My question is - I'm speaking about the part of the book that you authored and the events that you were involved in - did the editor change any names, any dates, or any specific time-lines that you provided?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one should go through my entire statement and not take individual sentences out of context. I think the editor, perhaps because he found it convenient, even changed some dates, but these changes make no difference to the essence of what was going on at the Vukovar Hospital in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said the editor changed some dates. What is the profession of this editor who was in charge of your book?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The editor was a well-known Croatian writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Based on what exactly did he change the dates, if your entries in this book represent your diary?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not my diary. I'm not sure if you read my book from cover to cover; if not, I can send you a copy. You have accounts day by day - this was published in the press - what was happening in the Vukovar area. It wasn't my own records because I never kept a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now fully understand the situation. If I tell you that in a portion of your book that you authored reads as follows: "Two APCs are firing their machine-guns and approaching the hospital." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: "They stopped and they trained their barrels on the hospital." That's the next sentence; is that correct? "The International Red Cross representative arrives and the tank disgorges a captain and a major, who are shouting: 'Everyone go back to the hospital. No one must leave the hospital.'" You're very specific. You talk about their ranks, a captain and a major shouting both at the same time and getting out of a tank. So is that correct or what you told us in your testimony here? Which is true?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that what I'm saying now is more accurate. As I've said, the editor took some words and sentences and I told him about the events. I told him about what had happened, that the APCs drove up. And I told him about what had happened, but he phrased these things his own way in the book and the book is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But are you absolutely convinced that what you're saying now is accurate? Here we have a writer who may be toying around with facts for his own reasons, and here we are dealing with facts. So could we say that this writer changed the facts altogether by inserting a JNA major whom you had never mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that Captain Radic had arrived and that he was followed by Major Sljivancanin, but I suppose the editor put it together as he liked and this is the result.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That means the editor changed this bit. We can move on now.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that's not the only bit that he changed. There is other things that we might discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Since you're adamant about this, what other notable changes did the editor make that were substantially different from what you had stated?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the book in front of me right now, nor am I able to comment on any details. If I could have the book and go through it again, then perhaps I could give you some feedback in terms of what I stated and what I did not state. I don't see this book as an accurate historical record. This is a personal account of something that happened, of people who suffered, of the suffering of those of us who were working at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This is a personal view, then; therefore, it's a witness account by someone who was in the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That means that we have witnesses in a courtroom, too, or what is being said. And the question is: Is your memory fresher and clearer now or back in 1992, early 1992, when the book was first published?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early 1992, the best part of those who had defended Vukovar were still in prisons or in camps, which you know full well, and this was the reason - and the editor did point this out at the time - that certain things cannot be recorded with a greatest possible accuracy and that's why he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about 13 years later? Did you not publish another book on the same subject in which you added all these details that you had not been aware of back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the name of Simo Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked at the hospital. I think he was a help worker but I'm not sure what his duties entailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: During these events, was he at the hospital too?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He showed up at the hospital, did what he was supposed to do, and then suddenly he disappeared. I have no idea where he had gone to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony on 1524 of the transcript dated the 11th of November, lines 4 to 8 - and this is something that you confirmed on a number of different occasions - you said: "On that evening, on the evening of the 18th of November, Bogdan Kuzmic and the captain inspected the hospital as well as the basement in which the wounded were." However, in this book - and I'm talking about a section of the book that you acknowledge as your own - you were asked on page 141, paragraph 2, whether you knew Simo Samardzic and you said - please confirm or deny - "Several hours after the army entered the hospital at about 1300 hours, suddenly the soldiers disappeared from all of the hospital's entrances, and the local imported Chetniks started coming in. I recognised some of those who had worked in the hospital. Bogdan Kuzmic, Simo Samardzic, they were going from bed to bed looking at the wounded. Very soon I found out why," and so on and so forth. And then you continue all the way up until the 19th. Not one single time in this book of yours -- or rather, can you comment on what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is a very liberal interpretation of the editor himself, who shaped my account into a text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But can you offer a logical explanation why you didn't say Bogdan Kuzmic, a JNA captain, went from one wounded to another and I knew why? But, rather, what we read here is that Kuzmic and Simo Samardzic did this and not Kuzmic and Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the reason the captain was not mentioned must be the fact that no person, no high-ranking soldier was mentioned during the rounds of the hospital on that day, with the exception of Bogdan Kuzmic and Simo Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I would be hard put to say I see a logical reason why in fact you didn't mention Captain Radic in the same context that you testified about here, but if you claim that this is another change that was made by the editor, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm not saying he changed that, but I believe it was later on the 20th that Captain Radic takes it from there. But we can talk about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that it wasn't Captain Radic who did this on the 18th but rather the 20th. What exactly is it you are trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this. I have no problems at all about cross-examining on a document, none at all, it's perfectly reasonable. But if in actual fact it's going to be done, my understanding from the Pre-Trial Conference was that if there was going to be reference to documentation, and in actual fact the documentation would be provided so that everybody knew exactly what was being referred to and we know what the point is. It's unfair if in actual fact the witness is merely cited in general terms parts of a book and never has sight of the part that's being referred to. And that was certainly my understanding of what was going to happen in cross-examination, both Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, it is the normal position that if you're cross-examining on a document and putting to the witness that his evidence differs from something said in that document at some earlier time by the witness, that you would allow the witness an opportunity to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue, perhaps one of the Court officials could accept this literary brain child, as it were, of Dr. Njavro, which I hope he will never disavow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the particular page, is it page 41, Mr. Borovic? Perhaps the doctor might --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically the page was 141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 141. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm now being shown this book. This book is not a document, rather, as I said, it was my personal view of what had happened at the hospital. I need to be given an opportunity to go through these things carefully, and therefore I would like to apply for a half-hour break in order to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, excuse me for interrupting, but I think this would be highly inappropriate at this point in time, in the middle of my cross-examination, to grant such a break as the witness has just requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Mr. Borovic. Doctor, if you would look at page 141, and refresh your recollection of that page, it's the second paragraph on page 141, I believe. If you just read that, and then you may be better able to answer Mr. Borovic as to whether that is in fact part of your writing or someone else's and whether -- if the account there is different from what you have said in evidence, why it is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Second paragraph, please. It's right there and the first word is "immediately" --

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the section that was highlighted in yellow here: "Several hours after the soldiers entered the hospital at 1300 hours, suddenly," and so on and so forth. And then it goes on to speak about Bogdan Kuzmic, Simo Samardzic, and others, and there is no mention of Captain Radic. I did mention him --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But if you look at this paragraph that you have in front of you, is there any reference to Captain Radic at all or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in this paragraph. There is no reference to Captain Radic, but there will be references to Captain Radic later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let's cross that bridge when we come to it. This paragraph you're looking at, is there any reference to the reservists Bogdan Kuzmic and Simo Samardzic inspecting the wounded and you concluding what the reason was for them doing that? Because that's what your book goes on to state. Do you stick to that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that statement, Bogdan Kuzmic was touring. I'm not sure about Simo Samardzic. That may have been added, but I'm certain about Bogdan Kuzmic but there was someone else with him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore would like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please, my next question is about the book, so in order to avoid going back and forth. Perhaps a little later, Mr. Prosecutor. You should have prepared for this case, you know -- just a joke, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's going too far, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November, that is your statement, Mr. Njavro, between 8.00 and 9.00, Captain Radic arrived and said, "From now on consider yourself arrested. You are not to leave this room." This is in the transcript and my learned friend the Prosecutor can check that. The 11th of November 2005, the page is 1523 and lines are 5 to 11. On the other hand, make sure you're following, you made a statement to the Prosecutor in 1995. The Prosecutor asked you in chief and you confirmed that you had indeed given this statement in 1995. In that statement you stated that the captain had told you: You are to stay here and you must not go anywhere. Nothing will happen to you. It is for your own safety that you are to remain here. As you see, first it says that he was arrested, but then the statement he gave to the OTP was that he had in fact been told that it was for his own safety that he was to remain in the room. Finally, please find page 141. I think that is the most important page, at least as regards this topic. It reads -- rather, would you be so kind as to read the bit that says "Major Sljivancanin" and on from there, the same paragraph where Kuzmic and Samardzic are mentioned. So it starts, "Major Sljivancanin then spoke to me."

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Major Sljivancanin then spoke to me. 'Doctor, I have a special conversation to have with you. You shall not to go anywhere and you will be escorted at all times. You are free to go on working at the hospital, but you are not to leave the building under any conditions.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My question is: Which of these two submissions is true? What do you think? What you testified here before this Court that you were arrested by Radic or the statement you gave to the OTP about a soldier who was looking after your safety in order to protect you from problems that you might otherwise have had? Or a third possibility where you mention to a third person who is telling you all these things? So which is true?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first version is true. What I stated before this Honourable Tribunal, what Captain Radic told me on the 19th, that is true. Major Radic, too, said something like this but that was on the 20th, so the dates are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: There is no date that you mention in that context the way you said it.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it's a little bit higher up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But you said Major Radic. Did you make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave it up to the Court to assess which one of your statements is true or correct. You also said that that morning, on the 19th of November, you complained to the captain, who had introduced himself as Captain Radic, that during the night the sick and the wounded were mistreated. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do we understand each other and can you explain to the Court in a logical manner why you complained to Captain Radic on the 19th in the morning if you're stating before the Tribunal that on the 18th of November in the evening it was precisely that same captain, according to what you said, who had abused the patients? So why were you complaining to him? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There was no other officer present in the hospital at the time, and why wouldn't I address him, referring amongst other things also to some military and Geneva Conventions which even though they were not respected, at least we were trying to refer to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: On the 19th, in the morning, you said that Kuzmic came to the hospital. You also stated - and we discussed this briefly a little bit earlier - that Marko Mandic disappeared from the hospital as well as some other drivers. In your statement to the OTP, on page 3, paragraph 8 - and I think the Prosecutor also referred you to that - you stated the following: "On the 18th of November the army arrived at the hospital and then after 5.00 the Chetniks did. They abused the wounded and the injured. I know that Bogdan Kuzmic took away a small group, and Marko Mandic was part of that group." So this was on the 17th, but earlier I read that you said that this was on the 19th, in the morning. Also, if he says that the hospital director, Vesna Bosanac -- and in the transcript of your statement and also for the OTP it was stated that on the 18th of the 11th -- the 18th of November, and I have the statement in front of you, maybe we can read that - this was also presented as an exhibit earlier. If I were to tell you that Vesna Bosanac stated the following: "Marko Mandic on the 18th of November in the evening, Marko Mandic and his wife, who was a nurse, together with a nurse and her husband, who was a police officer, left the medical centre Vukovar without my knowledge. However, Marko Mandic and his wife later returned." What is correct out of these three statements? Your statement, your earlier statement to the Prosecution, or the assertion by Vesna Bosanac regarding Marko Mandic? First of all, is Vesna Bosanac not stating the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object. This, I'm sure, is an unintentional error, but on my transcript I have got the reference to the OTP statement, referring to the 17th of November; I think that certainly is on the transcript. If I may just read -- there is reference to the -- "So this was on the 17th, but earlier I read that you said that this was on the 19th." Well, I'm sure it's unintentional, but that is not said in the statement that this occurred on the 17th at all. So I don't know how my learned friend can put a proposition to the witness that refers to the 17th when it says in -- as clear as one can anticipate it relates actually not to that date. It refers to the 18th and then moves on to about 5 p.m. and moves over to Marko Mandic being removed on the -- that's on page 4 of 7. Now, I know cross-examination can be difficult but this is an error, as far as I can see, and I can't see why it's occurring. And the witness is being given a false premise upon which to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, can I indicate that this problem is considerably aggravated because of the enormous length of what you put to the witness. It goes on for, at a rough guess, something like 20 lines; there seemed to be several different propositions in it. Can I suggest that you would get a lot further if you put each separate proposition to the witness one at a time and dealt with that, and then moved to the next one. And in that way, the witness will understand you more readily and will be able to respond to you more readily. And if it is that Mr. Moore is concerned about something you put, he can deal with it at that time rather than having to look back through this very long set of propositions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, I think that there is a mistake in the transcript, but I will present these three things very carefully to the witness, as I did earlier. The first thing is:

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you as a witness state here before this Tribunal that on the 19th of November in the morning Bogdan Kuzmic came to the hospital, and after that Marko Mandic disappeared from the hospital just like his drivers, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Second question: In your statement to the OTP, on page 3, paragraph 8, it states on the 18th of November, when you stated that Kuzmic came, after 5 p.m., to the hospital, is this indisputable?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We already spoke about that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said, "I know that Kuzmic took away a small group and Marko Mandic was in that group." That is the context of the statement you provided to the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this -- I don't have it in front of you [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you if that is correct, that statement.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I reply to that when I don't have the text in front of me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, if this is going to be done in the way that my learned friend suggests, he must allow it to be done accurately so the witness can deal with the issue, and it's not being done accurately. I understand Your Honour's point about re-examination, but it is not being done properly or accurately at this stage. And in my submission, that is unfair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, we certainly need assistance because things are not running smoothly and effectively at the moment from anybody's point of view. If you want the witness to comment on the accuracy of something said in a previous statement, you need to let him see that statement. It will be very rarely that a person can remember what is in a statement made some time in the past about a particular topic without seeing it. In fairness to the witness, he should be allowed to see it. So you need, if you're putting a previous statement to him, to show him the passage in the statement, and then get his reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I presented everything to the witness properly. Just one moment. I would -- I'll start from the back. Can we present the witness with the statement of Dr. Vesna Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would the witness be kind enough to read the entry of the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 18th in the evening, Marko Mandic and his wife, who was a nurse in the medical centre" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the original text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "-- with another nurse, and her husband, a police officer, left the medical centre Vukovar without my knowledge. I earlier instructed the medical staff not to leave the hospital because it could be dangerous for them outside. However, Marko Mandic and his wife later returned."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's make things brief and avoid presenting the witness with large chunks of text. In regard to what you said about Marko Mandic disappearing on the 19th, let's for the moment leave aside the statement that you gave to the OTP. Vesna Bosanac states that Marko Mandic left the hospital on the 18th, in the evening. You are telling the Court that on the 19th, in the morning, Marko Mandic disappeared and then you describe that. Is the statement by Vesna Bosanac incorrect or are you going to correct the statement that you provided here?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the statement of Dr. Vesna Bosanac confirms my statement because Marko Mandic and his wife later returned to the hospital, which means that on the 19th they were at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where does it state that they were in the hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a Latin saying, I don't want to repeat it here, but if it's said that they returned without her knowledge and without her permission -- however Marko Mandic and his wife, I stress - I'm sorry, I'm being a little bit loud - returned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If that is your answer, then thank you.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they spent the night at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the date that they spent at the hospital, of the night?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the night of the 19th, the night of the between the 18th and the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Marko on the 18th but not on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What time did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th in the evening I saw him. I don't know what time it was any more. I really cannot tell you with any certainty. It was dark, and I wasn't able to tell the time. I didn't have a watch, so it would be too much to ask me about exact -- the exact time. But I know that in the morning, after I was captured, those who were passing by said that Marko Mandic had been taken away, as well as a group of drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is as follows: But I'm not going to quote back to you your statement given to the OTP because there it doesn't say the 19th, it says the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have a clarification here by Dr. Vesna Bosanac, which I agree with, that he went on his own and then he later returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. That is your answer. Let's move on. Now I would like you to look at your book again. This is the most important part of the book that I would like to draw the Court's attention to, which will show that this witness did not speak the truth regarding these circumstances. The circumstances I'm thinking of refer to Captain Radic and the events on the 18th and the 19th, as well as the relationship between Dr. Njavro and Captain Radic. I'm looking at page 142. Would you kindly read line 7 from the top?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was approached" -- is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I was approached by the counter-intelligence service captain and he took me to the staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He was asking about certain dictionaries. He was interested in my -- certain doctors" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "-- and asked me about them. These were all doctors that used to work at the medical centre, at the surgical ward, who had left previously or had simply disappeared."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read five lines further.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He was particularly interested in a younger colleague, Dr. Radomir Dejanovic, general practitioner. He was asking about him." Well, this is important I would like to complete the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you already told the Court about this yesterday; there is no need to go into it again. Is that the same Radomir Dejanovic whom you mentioned yesterday before the -- during the hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, that's an appropriate question. I will listen to your questions about this passage now. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Radomir Dejanovic, whom you mentioned in your book, is that the same doctor whom you mentioned yesterday during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you say yesterday that Captain Radic showed interest in Dr. Radomir Dejanovic because they studied together?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Captain Radic asked me about Radomir Dejanovic, what I thought of him. And then, I don't know, he made a comment about their relations because allegedly they studied at the same time at the military academy and the medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really tell you exactly because I don't remember the exact conversation other than that question about Radovan [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Later in this text, some ten lines further, you say that the captain knew the doctor personally because they were friends from school.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've just explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So my question is now that you have read this and since you stated yesterday and today that Captain Radic was asking about Dr. Dejanovic at that time because they had studied together. My second question is: Where did Dr. Dejanovic study? But you told the Court yesterday that he studied in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember I think he mentioned that he studied in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you now - and the Prosecutor will perhaps assist me here, I have no doubt - that it can be seen from the indictment that Captain Radic studied in Sarajevo, would that indicate that you provided incorrect data and that Captain Radic actually was not there where you described him as being, that he didn't know Dr. Radomir Dejanovic, and that this is a mistaken -- case of mistaken identity?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about mistaken identity, if the exact words were said that I conveyed. It wasn't me asking him whom he knew among the doctors. I suppose he was talking about this person named Radomir Dejanovic at the time, discussing who studied where, but this is really not something that I can go into.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, really, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on his statement, based on what he said, I couldn't be certain, and I did make this clear in this passage. Maybe they did not study together, but that doesn't mean they didn't know each other. The captain introduced himself as Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, but I must interrupt you. We've heard about him introducing himself as Captain Radic over 50 times. What I'm asking you about is you provided an erroneous explanation here. You totally mixed up the two different persons, Captain KOS [as interpreted] and Captain Radic. And now you're using a lot of words and being very grandiloquent to avoid giving the answer that I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I said, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question: This counter-intelligence service captain who is supposed, in your account, to be Captain Radic, everything that you stated in relation to that points to that conclusion. My question is: Do you know that Captain Radic is a captain of the counter-intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've tried to say several times that the editor made additions in order to make for a more interesting read. So then the editor added certain observations and remarks of his own which I didn't object to at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Is this specifically something that the editor added or do you in fact know that Captain Radic was a captain of the counter-intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, how on earth would I have been expected to know that? But in all likelihood, at least judging on the basis of the time when we did our regular military service, all those who investigated things were, as a rule, suspected at least of being members of the counter-intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My opinion is you just haven't answered my question. Yet, let us move on, please. Yesterday we talked about the burning of paper. You answered that you only burned some of your personal papers.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, personal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Serbian word is "personal."

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And then I added another question yesterday about you burning documents in order to keep it from falling into the enemy's hands.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said "no," or as you have just confirmed, "no way." Can you please now again turn to your literary brain-child more specifically page 146 and read line 14. "As the army," and so on. 146, page 146.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 146. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It starts: "When the army entered" --

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Line 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: "When the army entered."

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When the army entered the hospital on the 18th of November, I had to burn some documents to keep them from falling into the enemy's hands," but this is something that we have discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You've just read it out. I'm cross-examining you now. You have provided a beautiful answer. You said three times over the last two days that you never burned any documents to keep it from falling into the enemy's hands, but rather just some personal documents. And now you've read this out. I'm asking you: Which is true, what your book says, your personal view, as you say, or what you testified in front of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I testified in front of the Trial Chamber and what I'm testifying now is as follows: I burned -- or rather not me, my wife did. I burned a number of personal documents, but by no means did I ever burn a single medical file that was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that this portion of the book, which says that you burned the documents to keep them from falling into the enemy's hands, is not accurate either, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how the book was produced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I couldn't remember accurately what I'd stated at the time and what the author eventually wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And who is the author?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The editor. The editor who placed his stamp of approval and gave the go ahead for the book to be printed. He's a very well-known writer in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We've heard that. But I can't agree with your statement that he is the author and not you, who put your name on the front page and had your photograph printed on the front of this piece. Would I be right in saying that you are, in fact, to be considered as the author of this book? We can see your photo on the front page and the author's name indicates that you were the person who authored this book and not somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. It's only logical that my photograph appeared on the front page. The intention, the idea in the editor's mind was to sell as many copies as possible, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The editor probably also wanted to make money by selling as many copies as possible. Wasn't that one of the things in his mind?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That must have been one of the objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Even at the cost of perhaps modifying or altering certain facts that you told him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think any substantial changes were made, with the exception of certain dates possibly, but the substance remains the same and was not altered. I think if you look at our discussion so far it reflects this truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I'm overstepping the mark in terms of time, Your Honour, so this may be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic, that's quite right. We will resume then at ten minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I could mention two small matters before we commence with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: They are really administrative matters. The first is I'm led to understand from the officer of the court that the doctor would wish to finish this evening, because Your Honour will remember that there is a commemoration service in Vukovar this week. That is the first matter, and I know that there is an element of concern about that. The second matter relates to Ambassador Okun. I've spoken to my learned friends. They believe that they will be, at the very least, the rest of the day and perhaps a little more. Of course Ambassador Okun is here; he's waiting to give evidence. But if in actual fact there is not a realistic likelihood of him commencing today, I would ask the Court's leave to release him. As I say, he's of mature years and it's a stressful event for him. Those are the two administrative matters and then there is a legal matter that I would wish to raise with the Court. I'll do them in whichever way Your Honour wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will deal with administration. I would take it that there would appear to be some sense in allowing the next witness to leave now and not waiting for the rest of today. I think that is a fair approach, given the way things have gone. The present witness, it appears, is anxious to be away so we will keep our delay of the cross-examination now as short as possible in the hope that it may be possible for counsel to deal with the matters that remain in the time that remains. I would ask the counsel that will be cross-examining and re-examining to keep the time in mind as much as they possibly can to accommodate the wishes of the doctor. Now, Mr. Moore, that legal question, must it be raised now or can it wait?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It can be dealt with now very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's quite simply this. The Status Conference was quite specific. If there was going to be cross-examination, that documents should be provided for the other side. There has been significant cross-examination on a document; we have not been provided with a copy. We have now been given a photocopy in B/C/S; it has now been taken back. And with the utmost respect to my learned friends, if they wish to have cooperation from the Prosecution, then the same principles must apply. And I would hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No need to say more, Mr. Moore. I have already indicated to counsel that if you're cross-examining on a document, you should have it available to so that the witness can see it. Clearly, it should also be available to the Prosecution and to other counsel. So if counsel would keep that in mind for future cross-examination, it will improve the flow of things and avoid the unnecessary delay or even the need for an adjournment. Having said that speedily, Mr. Borovic, if you would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The witness could help himself, too, by providing brief answers, if I may add. We shall, of course, do our best to serve onto the Prosecution all the documents in good time. Why has this occurred? We all know about the addenda to each and every witness's statements that appeared several hours before the examination, and we had to cope with it as we went along and take things in our stride. So that is the essence of the problem for us. Thank you for hearing me out on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When was the MUP building hit?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It must have been sometime in August, but I can't give you a specific date unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When the MUP building was hit, did members of the MUP and members of the ZNG, who you said were part of the MUP, run over to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this happening, but I think when the MUP building was damaged they went to a different shelter of the former Vupik, V-u-p-i-k, factory. It was a farming factory in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was this shelter near the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was near the hospital, almost as near as the MUP building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Is it almost part of the hospital compound?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really nearby -- not that near but very near.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said a while ago that there was an underground passage from the hospital which people could use to leave the hospital, and then there were two or three metres to cross before you reached the MUP building. What about this Vupik building, the underground shelter, is it in the same area as the MUP in relation to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was at the other end of the street. All the other residents and civilians were in that basement, all those who lived in that building, they were in that basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
